originalTitle: Big Chicken: A Fast Food Conspiracy review – Mo Gilligan ruffles feathers in battle against ultra-processed foods
summary: The ultra-likable comedian decides to go on a chicken shop diet for 28 days, but like a gen-Z Super Size Me uncovers some dark truths behind this billion-dollar industry
content: ‘I think you’re going to die,” says a teenager bluntly to comedian Mo Gilligan when he tells her about his plan to eat only from chicken shops for one month. Spoiler: he lives. But after 84 fried chicken meals, Gilligan is heavier, unhealthier and starting to feel depressed. In this funny, slick and accessible Netflix documentary he takes on “Big Chicken”, the industrialised poultry farming industry. Flavouring doc-journalism with his brand of ultra-likable humour, he’s gen Z’s answer to Michael Moore or Morgan Spurlock (who pulled a similar trick 20 years ago, eating nothing but McDonald’s for one month in his 2004 documentary Super Size Me). At the start of the film, there is no guilt in Gilligan’s pleasure walking into a chicken shop (“Bring on the wings!”). Growing up in a low-income household in London, a bucket of KFC was a family treat. He’s even done voiceover work for a Nando’s advert; “It’s just chickens, right?”. What works so well in the film is that Gilligan’s shock as he digs deeper into the industry doesn’t look manufactured for the camera. The UK rears one billion chickens a year and, in Lincolnshire, Gilligan meets animal welfare activists in balaclavas (“This is like Call of Duty. I’m scared!”). He learns about the environmental harm to rivers that chicken farming causes, and explores racist ideas around black people and fried chicken. In America, he investigates employment conditions in factories, workers denied toilet breaks forced to wear nappies. Back at his hotel, he bursts into tears; eating fried chicken for breakfast, lunch and dinner isn’t helping his mood. Gilligan speaks to a psychologist who explains how ultra-processed foods hook us, making us feel great – and then comes the crash. You can see the difference in Gilligan, who is lethargic and grumpy. It might not kill him, but his chicken diet is doing harm. The obvious objection to all this is that of course you’re not meant to eat fried chicken every day. But, as he finds out, half the calories in people’s diets in the UK come from ultra-processed foods and globally, there are now more obese children than hungry children. It’s probably fair to say Gilligan doesn’t uncover anything new in his film, but what he might succeed in is speaking to a new audience. At the very least it’s likely to encourage viewers to go cold chicken. • Big Chicken: A Fast Food Conspiracy is on Netflix from 5 August.
chineseTitle: 《大鸡：快餐阴谋》评论——莫·吉利根在与超加工食品的斗争中激怒了羽毛
chineseSummary: 这位超级讨人喜欢的喜剧演员决定进行 28 天的鸡肉店节食，但就像 Z 世代 Super Size Me 一样，揭露了这个价值数十亿美元的行业背后的一些黑暗真相
chineseContent: 当喜剧演员莫·吉利根 (Mo Gilligan) 告诉喜剧演员莫·吉利根 (Mo Gilligan) 计划一个月内只在鸡肉店里吃东西时，一名青少年直言不讳地说：“我觉得你快要死了。”剧透：他活了下来。但吃了 84 顿炸鸡后，吉利根变得更重、更不健康，并开始感到沮丧。在这部有趣、流畅且易于理解的 Netflix 纪录片中，他讲述了工业化家禽养殖业“大鸡”。超级讨人喜欢的幽默感，他是 Z 世代对迈克尔·摩尔 (Michael Moore) 或摩根·斯普尔洛克 (Morgan Spurlock) 的回应（20 年前，他在 2004 年的纪录片《Super Size Me》中，一个月只吃麦当劳）。 影片开头，吉利根在走进一家鸡肉店时毫无愧疚感（“带上翅膀！”）。甚至为 Nando 的广告做过画外音；“这只是鸡，对吗？”影片中吉利根的震撼之处在于，他深入研究了这个行业，而英国每年饲养 10 亿只鸡，在林肯郡，吉利根戴着头套与动物福利活动人士会面（“这就像《使命召唤》一样。我很害怕！”）。在美国，他调查了关于黑人和炸鸡的种族主义想法，回到酒店，他泪流满面；早餐、午餐和晚餐吃炸鸡对他的情绪没有帮助，他解释了超加工食品如何让我们感觉良好——然后你就可以看到吉利根的不同，他昏昏欲睡。
whyItMatters: 这条信息属于全球新闻信号，适合用于观察外部环境、政策变化、地缘风险和市场情绪。
